o: A substring is almost-palindromic if deleting exactly one character makes it a palindrome. Note a plain palindrome qualifies too (deleting any character leaves a palindrome). The key structural fact: if s[l..r] is almost-palindromic, so is s[l+1..r-1] (apply the same deletion inside). Hence for a fixed left endpoint l, the predicate P(r) = "s[l..r] is almost-palindromic" is monotone — once false, it stays false as r grows. That enables binary searching the largest feasible r for each l. In "abca" the whole string works (drop 'c'); in "abba" it is already a palindrome; in "zzabba" the best is "zabba" (drop the first 'z'). With n = 2500, n binary searches × O(n) verification is fast enough.
k: Deleting both endpoints of an almost-palindrome preserves the property — feasibility is monotone in r for fixed l.
Verification is the classic two-pointer with one skip: at the first mismatch, try deleting either side and require a strict palindrome afterward.
Plain palindromes count, so the answer is at least 1.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Substrings
a.i: Check every (l, r) pair with the one-deletion verifier. Simple and obviously correct; serves as the baseline against which the optimized version is validated, though it may be slow near the constraint ceiling.
s: Write isPal(l, r): strict palindrome check via two pointers.
Write almost(l, r): scan inward; on first mismatch at (a, b), return isPal(a+1, b) or isPal(a, b-1); if no mismatch, return true.
Take the maximum r - l + 1 over all pairs passing almost().
a.t: O(n³) worst case — O(n²) pairs each verified in O(n).

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Search on Right Endpoint
a.i: Exploit monotonicity: shrinking an almost-palindromic substring from both ends keeps it almost-palindromic, so for each l the set of valid r is a prefix of [l, n-1]. Binary search the boundary using the O(n) verifier, cutting the pair enumeration to n log n verifications.
s: Implement the same isPal and almost helpers.
For each l, binary search the largest r in [l, n-1] with almost(l, r) true.
Update the answer with r - l + 1 whenever feasible.
a.t: O(n² log n) worst case — n binary searches, each doing O(log n) verifier calls of O(n); typically far faster in practice.

w: Lead with the monotonicity observation — it is the crux interviewers look for. Pitfalls: assuming a greedy single-side deletion suffices at a mismatch (both sides must be tried), forgetting palindromes themselves qualify, and minimum-length edge cases (answer ≥ 1 always). Follow-ups: allow k deletions (the verifier generalizes to a bounded-mismatch recursion), or return the substring itself rather than its length.
